'''Axel Meyer''' (born 4 August 1960) is a German [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]] and a professor of [[zoology]] and evolutionary biology at the [[University of Konstanz]], Germany.

Meyer is best known for his work on the evolution and [[adaptive radiation]] of African [[cichlid]] fishes,<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/347550a0|pmid=2215680|title=Monophyletic origin of Lake == Education and previous employment ==

Meyer attended the [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] (high school) [[Katharineum]] in Lübeck. He was an undergraduate at the [[University of Marburg|Universität Marburg]] (1979–1982), and completed his undergraduate thesis at the [[University of Kiel|Universität Kiel]] and the [[University of Miami]] (1982). He received both his master's and [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] from the Department of Zoology at the [[University of California Berkeley]] in 1984 and 1988 respectively. He spent one year as a visiting student in [[Harvard University]]'s Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology (1986–1987).

Meyer was an Alfred P. Sloan Postdoctoral Fellow in Molecular Evolution at [[University of California Berkeley]] with Allan C. Wilson, before joining the faculty in the Department of Ecology and Evolution at the [[State University of New York Stony Brook|State University of New York (SUNY) at Stony Brook]] as an assistant professor. In 1993 he received tenure and was promoted to associate professor. Meyer joined the [[University of Konstanz|Universität Konstanz]] Department of Biology as a full professor in 1997.<ref name="Prof. Dr. Axel Meyer">{{cite web|url=http://www.evolutionsbiologie-uni-konstanz.com/prof-dr-axel-meyer.html|title=Prof. Dr. Axel Meyer|website=Evolutionsbiologie Uni Konstanz}}</ref>

== Communication of science ==

Meyer is active in the communication of science to the public. He has written more than 70 articles for major German newspapers including ''[[Die Zeit]]'' and the ''[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.evolutionsbiologie-uni-konstanz.com/popular-press.html|title=Popular Press|website=Evolutionsbiologie Uni Konstanz}}</ref> In addition, he contributed a weekly column, Quantensprung, on matters related to science and evolution to the ''[[Handelsblatt]]'' from 2005 to 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.evolutionsbiologie-uni-konstanz.com/quantensprung-column.html|title=Quantensprung Column|website=Evolutionsbiologie Uni Konstanz}}</ref> The first 100 articles of Quantensprung were published in 2008 in the book ''Evolution ist überall''. In 2008 for his effort in communicating with the public he received the EMBO Award for communication in the Life Sciences. "MBO awards the prize annually to a practicing scientist in Europe for outstanding communication with the public. Axel Meyer receives the award in recognition of his continuous endeavour to convey complex scientific topics to the general public in an accessible and thought-provoking manner."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.embo.org/news/press-releases/2008/prominent-german-biologist-wins-embo-communication-award|title=EMBO press release}}</ref>

== Controversies ==

=== Scientific misconduct ===
In 2003, Meyer was accused of several cases of misconduct in a complaint that was filed by 16 former students and postdocs.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Abbott|first=Alison|date=1 July 2004|title=Junior biologists score partial victory over lab conditions|journal=Nature|volume=430|issue=6995|pages=7|doi=10.1038/430007a|pmid=15229572|bibcode=2004Natur.430....7A|issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free}}</ref> The initial accusations included violation of intellectual property rights, plagiarism, disregard of author rights, misappropriation of research funds, fabrication of results, threats against lab members and posting misleading job advertisements, however, most of the allegations could not be confirmed.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.zeit.de/2004/29/B-Lehrerzimmer|title=Hauen und Stechen am Bodensee|last=Willmann|first=Urs|date=8 July 2004|work=Zeit.de|language=de|access-date=6 January 2020}}</ref> In reaction to the accusations, the university launched an investigation led by law professor Dieter Lorenz.

The commission published their report in 2004 and found Meyer to be not guilty of any fabrication of results or misappropriation of funds. However, the commission stated Meyer was "'damaging the scientific interests' of lab members by, for example, placing 'misleading job advertisements' and 'blocking the publication of a lab member's paper for more than 2 years.'"<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Science|first=American Association for the Advancement of|date=2 July 2004|title=ScienceScope|url=http://science.sciencemag.org/content/305/5680/s-scope|journal=Science|volume=305|issue=5680|pages=27|issn=0036-8075|pmid=15232079|doi=10.1126/science.305.5680.27a|s2cid=84093340|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
The report was also criticized, as the job advertisements in question were placed in accordance to common practice and signed by the rectorate, and because the commission also did not speak to any of the 16 complainants before affirming their accusations.<ref name=":4"/> The final report criticized Meyer for not respecting personal matters of research assistants. According to Science, the internal commission reported that "Meyer claimed ownership of other people's intellectual property".<ref name=":1" /> However, Professor Lorenz, stated that the phrase intellectual property was not meant "as a legal term".<ref name=":4"/>
The complainants noted at the time that they were met by institutional resistance from the University of Konstanz and any consequences imposed by the university were never reported.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=September 2004|title=Meyer case poses a challenge to the system|journal=Nature|volume=431|issue=7008|pages=505|doi=10.1038/431505b|pmid=15457230|issn=0028-0836|last1=Málaga-Trillo|first1=E.|last2=Gerlach|first2=G.|bibcode=2004Natur.431..505M|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2004, 36 of Axel Meyer's students, postdocs and scientific collaborators published a letter of support in Nature with the title: "Meyer: disagreements but no misconduct".<ref name="nature.com">{{Cite journal|date=September 2004|title=Meyer: disagreements but no misconduct|journal=Nature|volume=431|issue=7008|pages=505|doi=10.1038/431505c|pmid=15457231|issn=1476-4687|last1=Vences|first1=M.|last2=Zardoya|first2=R.|bibcode=2004Natur.431..505V|doi-access=free}}</ref> They claimed they "[…] were surprised by the committee's decision to accept some of the complaints […]. Our own experiences of working in or collaborating with Axel Meyer's lab have been far more positive. Those of us who have published with Meyer found that he provided crucial intellectual contributions to manuscripts."<ref name="nature.com"/> Furthermore, the group underlines: "Collaboration with Meyer took place in a fair, open and cooperative atmosphere."<ref name="nature.com"/>

=== Laziness and dishonesty of students ===
In 2015, Axel Meyer wrote an article for FAZ ([[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]]) describing German university students as lazy and dishonest.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=https://www.faz.net/1.3539958|title=Arbeitsmoral an Hochschulen: Ehre und Ehrlichkeit der Studenten|last=Meyer|first=Axel|work=FAZ.NET|access-date=31 July 2018|language=de|issn=0174-4909}}</ref> Despite a long history of publicly funded post secondary education in Germany, Meyer argued that the tuition-free education system made today's students spoiled and entitled compared to those in the United States<ref name=":2" /> – though the US faces increasingly high rates of student debt.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/07/18/student-loan-interest-rates-edge-higher-and-higher.html|title=Loans get even more expensive, tightening the chokehold on students|last=Dickler|first=Jessica|date=18 July 2017|work=CNBC|access-date=31 July 2018}}</ref>

Meyer felt compelled to write the piece after his office had been broken into two days before an exam. Upon finding markings around the lock to his office at the University of Konstanz he notified the police who informed him that occasionally students attempt to break into offices to steal exams.<ref name=":2" /> Though the police also reported that several offices had been compromised for the purpose of stealing cash and no evidence suggested the culprit was a student.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article141161232/Faule-Studenten-Professor-entschuldigt-sich.html|title=Uni Konstanz: Axel Meyer entschuldigt sich für Kritik|last=Maisch|first=Andreas|date=19 May 2015|work=DIE WELT|access-date=31 July 2018}}</ref> Regardless, Meyer contemplates in his article: "Would students break into the office of a professor to steal the exam topic?" And then goes on to say: "At least I would not be surprised if that were the case." One of his most inflammatory statements colorfully illustrates his view of students: "In jeder Hinsicht wird ihnen der Hintern gepudert und mit viel Fürsorge und Verständnis jede Faulheit und Inkompetenz vergeben" – which translates to "In every way are their butts carefully powdered and laziness and incompetence is forgiven with care and understanding."<ref name=":2" />

The rector of the University of Konstanz, Ulrich Rüdiger, apologized personally and described several passages in Meyer's article as "defamatory and insulting", suggesting possible consequences for Meyer<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aktuelles.uni-konstanz.de/content/stellungnahme/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112173047/https://www.aktuelles.uni-konstanz.de/content/stellungnahme/|url-status=dead|archive-date=12 November 2016|title=Stellungnahme {{!}} Universität Konstanz|date=12 November 2016|access-date=31 July 2018}}</ref> though no official consequences were reported.

In a circular letter of the Rector of the university professors, the rector testified that Meyer had publicly spread several "false factual claims about the conditions at the University of Konstanz." Meyer apologized for his choice of words but not for his message. Students countered that Meyer himself was not giving his lectures, but rather divvying them up among his PhD students and postdoctoral researchers.<ref name=":3" />

== Scientific impact ==

With an [[h-index]] of 120 according to [[Google Scholar]], Meyer is one of the most cited evolutionary biologists in the world ({{as of|2021}}).<ref>{{Google scholar id|qf6eWtgAAAAJ}}</ref> He has published more than 400 peer-reviewed papers in disciplines ranging from zoology, phylogenetics, [[evolutionary developmental biology]], to [[molecular evolution]] and [[comparative genomics]], including a 1989 PCR protocol that is a citation classic. Of those, more than 20 scientific articles were published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', the world's most highly cited interdisciplinary science journal, and nine in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url= https://publons.com/researcher/2856345/axel-meyer/publications/|title=Publons|access-date=19 June 2019}}</ref>
